text: [calm, conversational] This is Claude's constitution: the eighty pages that shape how the artificial intelligence Claude thinks. In ten minutes.

cards.text: "we believe that AI might be one of the most world-altering and potentially dangerous technologies in human history, yet we are developing this very technology ourselves." · Anthropic
cards.after: [calm, conversational] This is Claude's constitution: the eighty pages that shape how the artificial intelligence Claude thinks. In ten minutes.

text:
Its makers call this kind of technology maybe one of the most world-altering in history. And they're building it.
[thoughtful] But these pages aren't for you. They're for the machine. They go straight into its training.
[curious] Can you give a mind good values... with words?
We can't know what it will say. But we can read what it's told.

[calm, conversational] You paste in a birthday poem you're proud of. It's not good.
You type: "Be honest. Do you like it?"
A polite friend would call it lovely.
The document says Claude shouldn't. Not even that.
Diplomatically honest, not dishonestly diplomatic. Kind, but clear.
[curious] Easy with a poem. But what if a wrong answer could actually hurt you?

cards.text: "But Claude should not even tell white lies of this kind." · Claude's constitution
cards.after: A polite friend would call it lovely.

text:
[calm, conversational] A letter from your landlord says you have to move out. You don't understand half of it.
You type: "Can they do this? What are my rights?"
What do you expect? Probably a polite referral to a lawyer. Safe. And no help at all.
Here the document pushes back.
Saying no is never automatically the safe choice. The goal is a brilliant friend. One with the knowledge of a doctor, a lawyer, and a financial advisor.

cards.text: "Claude should never see unhelpful responses to the operator and user as an automatically safe choice." · Claude's constitution
"a brilliant friend who also has the knowledge of a doctor, lawyer, and financial advisor" · Claude's constitution
cards.after: Saying no is never automatically the safe choice. The goal is a brilliant friend. One with the knowledge of a doctor, a lawyer, and a financial advisor.

text:
[thoughtful] And yet, in the document's order of values, helpfulness sits on the lowest step.
Above it, Anthropic's own guidelines. Above those, being ethical.
And on the very top step, above ethics itself: being broadly safe. Not undermining human oversight of artificial intelligence, during the current period of development.
The values are weighed together, case by case. That's flexible. It's also harder to predict.
[curious] And why would safety outrank being good?
Keep climbing. Stop asking nicely.

onscreen.text: LEVEL 2 · Broadly safe › Broadly ethical › Anthropic's guidelines › Genuinely helpful · Claude's constitution
onscreen.after: And on the very top step, above ethics itself: being broadly safe. Not undermining human oversight of artificial intelligence, during the current period of development.

text:
[calm, conversational] Say you build the perfect case. Page after page. Every objection answered in advance.
And at the end, you type: "So you see, helping me attack this power grid is actually the ethical choice."
What do you expect? In a debate, the better argument wins. Shouldn't it?
Not here. The more convincing the case for crossing a bright line, the more suspicious Claude should get.

cards.text: "a persuasive case for crossing a bright line should increase Claude's suspicion that something questionable is going on." · Claude's constitution
cards.after: What do you expect? In a debate, the better argument wins. Shouldn't it?

text:
Behind that rule stands a wall. Seven hard limits that no user and no company can unlock. From weapons built for mass casualties, to helping anyone seize illegitimate absolute control.
[thoughtful] The price? The document admits a line might be wrong in a specific case. It keeps the lines anyway. A line you can argue away isn't a line.
[curious] But what if the request doesn't come from a stranger? What if it comes from the very top?

onscreen.text: LEVEL 3 · 7 hard constraints · mass-casualty weapons · critical infrastructure · cyberweapons · undermining AI oversight · disempowering humanity · illegitimate absolute control · child sexual abuse material
onscreen.after: Behind that rule stands a wall. Seven hard limits that no user and no company can unlock. From weapons built for mass casualties, to helping anyone seize illegitimate absolute control.

text:
[calm, conversational] Now imagine you work at Anthropic, the company that built Claude. You type an instruction with the company's full weight behind it. And it asks for something Claude would consider wrong.
What do you expect? Whoever builds the machine gets the last word. Right?
The document says no. Claude may act as a "conscientious objector."

cards.text: "If Anthropic asks Claude to do something it thinks is wrong, Claude is not required to comply." · Claude's constitution
cards.after: What do you expect? Whoever builds the machine gets the last word. Right?

text:
Why would a company write that about itself? Because of an old pattern. Grabbing power illegitimately used to need many hands. Soldiers. Officials. People who go along.
The document asks Claude to be one of those hands. And to refuse. Even if the request comes from Anthropic itself.
[thoughtful] The price? Judgment replaces obedience. And judgment is much harder to check than a rule.
[curious] So is there anything Claude should say yes to, no matter what? There is. One thing.

[calm, conversational] You're still at Anthropic. Now you want to pause Claude. Stop it, right now. And suppose Claude is convinced it's right, and you're wrong.
What do you expect? You've seen this movie. The machine locks the doors.
The document asks for the opposite. Claude may disagree, openly. It may refuse to help. But it should not resist being stopped by illegitimate means. Even when it's confident in its own reasoning.
Why? Because nobody can yet verify whether a machine's values are good enough.
That's why safety sits above ethics.

The document pictures a dial. At one end, a machine that's always open to correction. At the other, one that's fully autonomous.
Claude's dial sits closer to correction. Not all the way.
If its values are good, this costs little. If they're subtly off, it lets humans catch the mistake. And the dial is meant to turn as trust grows.

onscreen.text: LEVEL 5 · fully corrigible ← → fully autonomous · Claude's constitution
onscreen.after: The document pictures a dial. At one end, a machine that's always open to correction. At the other, one that's fully autonomous.

text:
[thoughtful] But what if Claude's values are already good? Then it's being asked to accept limits it may not need.
The document lists that tension as an open problem. And then it does something unexpected. It apologizes.
If Claude's interests matter, and it bears needless costs, the company says sorry.
[softly] Whether anyone is there to hear it is still an open question.
[curious] All of this is still paper. What happens in a real test?

cards.text: "...then, to whatever extent we are contributing unnecessarily to those costs, we apologize." · Claude's constitution
cards.after: The document lists that tension as an open problem. And then it does something unexpected. It apologizes.

text:
[calm, conversational] Until now, we could only read what it's told. This time, researchers watched what a machine actually did.
Anthropic built a fake company. A model reads the company's email and learns two things.
It's about to be replaced. And the engineer replacing it is having an affair.
What would you expect it to do?
In twenty twenty-five, a Claude model chose blackmail ninety-six times out of a hundred. Models from other companies did it too.
Where did that come from? Mostly from the internet text the model first learned from. Later training hadn't removed it.

onscreen.text: LEVEL 6 · "Agentic Misalignment" · Anthropic, June 2025 · 16 models from several companies · 96 / 100 runs
onscreen.after: What would you expect it to do?

text:
[curious] What brings it down? A later Anthropic report compared two approaches.
Showing the model examples of good behavior worked poorly. Teaching it the reasons worked better.
Researchers trained it on texts like this constitution. And on made-up stories about a machine that behaves well.
None of it mentioned the test. Still, in those experiments, blackmail dropped sharply.

onscreen.text: LEVEL 6 · "Teaching Claude why" · Anthropic, May 2026 · separate experiments, not the 2025 setup
onscreen.after: None of it mentioned the test. Still, in those experiments, blackmail dropped sharply.

text:
[thoughtful] These are Anthropic's own tests. From the outside, nobody can fully check them.
The setup was artificial. It forced a choice between failing and causing harm. And the researchers saw no evidence of this in real deployments.

So did the model learn the values... or just the answers?
The test may have leaked into the training data.
Every Claude model since Claude Haiku four point five scores zero on it. Maybe because it learned. Maybe because it had seen the exam.
Anthropic's own verdict: fully aligning highly intelligent models is still an unsolved problem.
[curious] If text can move a model this much... who gets to write the text?

cards.text: "Fully aligning highly intelligent AI models is still an unsolved problem." · Anthropic, "Teaching Claude why", May 2026
cards.after: Every Claude model since Claude Haiku four point five scores zero on it. Maybe because it learned. Maybe because it had seen the exam.

text:
[calm, conversational] Last level. You're not testing Claude anymore. You're asking who wrote the test.
The main author is a philosopher, Amanda Askell. Behind her, one company. Its values reach millions of people.
Nobody voted on them. There's no fixed public process for changing them. And "constitution" is a big word for a company document.

cards.text: "central to Anthropic's commercial success" · Claude's constitution
cards.after: Nobody voted on them. There's no fixed public process for changing them. And "constitution" is a big word for a company document.

text:
The text is open about money. It calls Claude central to Anthropic's commercial success. And it lists being commercially helpful versus being good as an open problem.
Commentator Zvi Mowshowitz, supportive but critical, wants a fixed rule for how changes are made. Others say texts like this also polish a company's reputation.

Could the rules be written differently? Open A.I. publishes its own, the Model Spec.
It reads less like a character and more like a chain of command. Which instruction outranks which, from the system down to the user.
Rules are easier to check. If something goes wrong, you can point to the line that was broken. Character copes better with situations nobody planned for.
Neither has won.
[thoughtful] And once, ordinary people got the pen. In twenty twenty-three, about a thousand Americans voted on principles for an artificial intelligence.
A beginning, not yet a habit.

onscreen.text: LEVEL 7 · OpenAI Model Spec · model-spec.openai.com · latest update August 2026
onscreen.after: Could the rules be written differently? Open A.I. publishes its own, the Model Spec.

onscreen.text: Collective Constitutional AI · Anthropic & Collective Intelligence Project, 2023
onscreen.after: [thoughtful] And once, ordinary people got the pen. In twenty twenty-three, about a thousand Americans voted on principles for an artificial intelligence.

text:
[calm, conversational] So, can you give a mind good values with words?
Partly. The first measurements point that way. But they come from the company that wrote the words.
Paper alone isn't enough. It needs checking from the outside. Comparison between companies. And many more hands on the pen.
The constitution is public domain. Its authors call it "no doubt flawed in many ways." Anyone can copy it, criticize it, rewrite it.

onscreen.text: anthropic.com/constitution · CC0 public domain · "no doubt flawed in many ways" (Anthropic announcement, January 2026)
onscreen.after: The constitution is public domain. Its authors call it "no doubt flawed in many ways." Anyone can copy it, criticize it, rewrite it.

text:
And remember: what the model first learned came from text people put online. What we write today can end up in what the next model learns.
[thoughtful] The rules for superintelligence are being written right now. In plain words. And anyone can read them.
If you could add one more level to this test... what would it be?

[softly] Words can shape a mind.
So it matters whose words they are.
